1001328.etyen:
Borrowed from German Erna, a short form of Ernestine and Ernesta, feminine names derived from Ernst, ultimately from Old High German ernust (“serious, earnest”). First attested in the 18th century in Norway.
The name is identical in form to Old Norse Erna, the name of Jarl's wife in the poem Rígsþula, traditionally connected with ern (“brisk, vigorous, hale”). It is uncertain whether this Old Norse name independently influenced modern Norwegian usage.
Compare Danish Erna and Swedish Erna (“female given names”).

1004912.etyen:
From fag (“field, profession”) + konferanse (“conference”), literally “professional-field conference”.
The first element, fag (“field, subject, profession”), is borrowed from Low German fak (“compartment, field”), originally referring to something delimited or joined together and later developing the sense “field, discipline, profession”. The second element, konferanse (“conference”), is borrowed through French conférence (“conference”) from Medieval Latin conferentia (“meeting, consultation”), from confero (“to bring together; confer”), itself from con- (“together”) + fero (“to carry, bear”),
